title: Ethernet & MAC Addressing
summary: Learn the Ethernet frame format, how MAC addresses are structured, and why VLANs and switched full-duplex links reshaped how shared media used to work.

slides.markdown: **Ethernet** is the near-universal data link protocol for wired LANs, and every device on one has a **MAC address** — a globally unique, hardware-burned identifier used for local delivery. This topic covers the frame format, the address itself, and how switching quietly made an entire class of collision problems disappear.

An Ethernet II frame wraps the IP packet in link-layer addressing and a CRC:

![Ethernet II frame: preamble, destination MAC, source MAC, EtherType, payload up to the MTU, and FCS](assets/ethernet-frame-format.svg)

The **MTU** (Maximum Transmission Unit) of 1500 bytes is the payload cap — a bigger IP packet has to be fragmented before it fits in one frame.

assets.alt: Ethernet II frame: preamble, destination MAC, source MAC, EtherType, payload up to the MTU, and FCS

slides.markdown:
A **MAC address** is 48 bits, written as six hex byte-pairs (`3C:22:FB:A1:9E:04`). It splits into two halves:

- **First 3 bytes — OUI** (Organizationally Unique Identifier): assigned to the manufacturer by the IEEE. `3C:22:FB` might be Apple, `00:1A:2B` might be Cisco.
- **Last 3 bytes — NIC-specific**: assigned by the manufacturer itself, unique per device they make.

This means you can identify a device's vendor just by its OUI prefix — useful for network inventory and, less charitably, for device fingerprinting.

On old shared-medium Ethernet (one coax cable, or a hub), only one device could transmit at a time without garbling the signal. **CSMA/CD** managed this:

1. **Carrier sense** — listen before transmitting; if busy, wait.
2. **Collision detection** — if two devices transmit anyway, both detect the garbled signal.
3. **Backoff** — both stop, wait a random time, retry — randomness avoids colliding again immediately.

Same idea as raising your hand before speaking, then waiting your turn if you talk over someone.

Modern switched Ethernet gives each device its own dedicated **full-duplex** link to the switch — send and receive on separate wire pairs, simultaneously, with no other device sharing that segment. There's no shared medium left to contend for, so there's nothing for CSMA/CD to detect.

CSMA/CD hardware is technically still part of the Ethernet standard for backward compatibility, but on virtually every modern switched network it never activates — collisions on a full-duplex switched link are structurally impossible, not just rare.

Layer 2 addressing supports three delivery patterns:

- **Unicast** — one specific destination MAC, delivered to exactly one device.
- **Broadcast** — the all-ones address `FF:FF:FF:FF:FF:FF`, delivered to every device in the broadcast domain (used by ARP requests, DHCP discovery).
- **Multicast** — a reserved address range, delivered to any device that's subscribed to that multicast group (used by some routing protocols and streaming applications).

A switch treats these differently: unicast gets forwarded to one learned port; broadcast and unregistered multicast get flooded to every port.

**802.1Q VLAN tagging** lets one physical switch behave as multiple logically separate broadcast domains — a 4-byte tag inserted into the frame marks which VLAN it belongs to:

![One switch split into two isolated VLANs — HR and Engineering — via 802.1Q tags](assets/vlan-tagging.svg)

This is why a company can put Finance, Engineering, and Guest Wi-Fi on the same physical switches without any of them seeing each other's broadcast traffic.

assets.alt: One switch split into two isolated VLANs — HR and Engineering — via 802.1Q tags

slides.markdown:
| | MAC address | IP address |
|---|---|---|
| Layer | Data link (2) | Network (3) |
| Scope | Local — one link/segment | Global — routable across networks |
| Changes hop-to-hop? | Rewritten at every hop | Stays the same end to end |
| Assigned by | Manufacturer (burned in) | Network admin/DHCP, per network |

**How to decide which to reason about:** if the question is "how does this get from network to network," think IP; if it's "how does this get delivered on this one wire/segment," think MAC.

**Jumbo frames** raise the MTU beyond the standard 1500 bytes (often to 9000), reducing per-packet header overhead for high-throughput links like storage networks or data-center backbones.

The catch: every device along the path — every switch, every NIC — has to agree on the same MTU. If one hop silently doesn't support jumbo frames, large packets get dropped without an obvious error, showing up as mysterious performance cliffs on specific traffic sizes rather than a clean failure.

slides.sectionTitle: MAC addresses don't route across the internet
slides.subTitle: "Why can't I just send to a MAC address across the world?"
slides.markdown:
A common mistake is assuming MAC addresses could, in principle, be used to reach a device anywhere on the internet — they can't. MAC addresses have **no hierarchical structure tied to location**; a router has no way to look up "which direction is `3C:22:FB:A1:9E:04`" the way it can with an IP prefix.

This is exactly why routing exists at layer 3: IP addresses are allocated in structured, aggregatable blocks that scale to routing tables with a few hundred thousand entries, not billions of individual flat MAC addresses.
